segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: the rasa night. Pride, and Krishna vanished; set it down, and see who's beside you. Today, the jnana road, and three of its boldest words.

A herd of cows. They give milk, they pull the cart, they are a family's living. Suppose one wanders off one day, free. For the owner, losing even one is a nuisance, and losing many is worse. Here's the strange part. An Upanishad says the gods see people that way. It's not pleasing to the gods, it says, that people should come to know this. Know what? Three words.
screen: `A HERD OF COWS.` → `ONE WANDERS OFF, FREE.` → `THE GODS WOULD RATHER YOU DIDN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tells it like a creation story. In the beginning, this world was Brahman, the ultimate reality. And it knew itself, saying: aham brahmasmi. I am Brahman. By knowing that, it became everything. Whoever awakens to this, the text says, among the gods, the sages or people, becomes that. Even now, whoever knows I am Brahman becomes all this, and even the gods can't stop them, because that person has become the gods' own Self. But someone who worships a god thinking, he is one and I am another, doesn't know, the text says. Then the cow line: just as many cows serve a person, each person serves the gods, and losing even one cow is unpleasant. So the gods aren't pleased when people learn this. It's a startling, almost funny picture, pointing at something serious: in the text, whoever knows this can't be held back, not even by the gods. Aham brahmasmi is one of the four great sayings, the mahavakyas, beside the tat tvam asi you met with the salt and the seed. Tat tvam asi is the teacher saying: you are that. Aham brahmasmi is the student finally saying it from the inside: I am. Different schools hear it differently. Advaita hears strict identity. Ramanuja's and Madhva's followers read the same line within their own views, where the soul stays distinct and devotion stays whole. On the jnana road, the line is less a claim to argue than a place to look from.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING, BRAHMAN KNEW ITSELF.` · `WHOEVER KNOWS THIS BECOMES ALL.` · `THE GODS AREN'T PLEASED.` · `YOU ARE THAT, THEN: I AM.` · then, large: `AHAM BRAHMĀSMI.`

segments.voice: Say the word I silently, once, and notice where it seems to come from: not your name, not your job, not your story, just the plain sense of I am, here, now. Rest in that, and let every label fall away for a breath; if one comes back, that's fine, notice it and return to the simple sense of being. You don't have to believe anything, just look, and if you pray, you can rest in God as the ground of that I.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. On the jnana road the action is knowing, and in the Upanishad, whoever knows I am Brahman can't be held back, even by the gods.
Your line: drop every label, and feel: I am. No label needed for that one. Day three hundred thirteen, done.
